summary: Provides test vectors for several STUN attributes, FINGERPRINT, MESSAGE-INTEGRITY, and XOR-MAPPED-ADDRESS, whose values involve hashing and XOR. Implementers use them to check their code. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When you build a calculator, you try problems with known answers. This document gives known answers for STUN's math so programmers can check their work.

subtitle: Reference data for testing STUN implementations.

tldr.problem: Implementations of STUN must perform hashing and XOR operations on messages, but these operations are error-prone. Implementers need a reliable way to verify their code works correctly.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC provides sample STUN messages with known correct values for FINGERPRINT (CRC32 checksums), MESSAGE-INTEGRITY (HMAC-SHA1 hashes), and XOR-MAPPED-ADDRESS attributes, along with the input values and expected results.
tldr.outcome: Developers can run these test vectors through their implementations to catch bugs in cryptographic operations, which would otherwise be discovered only in the field.

facts.label: Message types covered
facts.value: Requests and IPv4 and IPv6 responses

today: RFC 5769 is an Informational Standard providing test vectors for STUN implementations. It has not been obsoleted. The vectors remain widely used for validating STUN library implementations and are often included in test suites for NAT traversal software.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 5389 defines STUN (Session Traversal Utilities for NAT), a protocol for discovering network address translation, learning public IP addresses, and traversing firewalls. STUN messages include cryptographic checksums and transformed addresses to verify data integrity and hide sensitive information.

This document provides test vectors: sample STUN messages with correct cryptographic values. The three STUN attributes most prone to implementation errors are FINGERPRINT (a CRC32 check), MESSAGE-INTEGRITY (an HMAC-SHA1 authentication code), and XOR-MAPPED-ADDRESS (a transformed IP address). The test vectors allow implementers to verify their hashing and XOR code.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a cookbook of recipe ingredients and results. Coders follow the recipe and compare their output to these answers to prove they got it right.

sections.title: Sample Messages and Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC provides four example STUN messages in hexadecimal format, representing common real-world use cases. The first is a request from a client using ICE (Interactive Connectivity Establishment) with username and password. The second and third are IPv4 and IPv6 responses with address translation.

Each message shows all binary bytes and labels each attribute. The examples include the SOFTWARE attribute, PRIORITY for ICE, and ICE-CONTROLLED for role determination. All messages are formatted exactly as a STUN peer would generate or process them, with precise byte positions and padding bytes.

The fourth example tests long-term credential authentication, a different mode where the server challenges the client with a nonce and realm. This example includes Unicode characters in the username to test internationalization handling.
sections.plainLanguage: Here are four example letters written in a special code. Each one has all the parts a real letter would have: addresses, stamps, and signatures. You can decode them and check if your answer matches.

sections.title: Using the Test Vectors
sections.content:
To use these vectors, extract the hexadecimal message bytes and input them to a STUN implementation. The implementation should parse the message, verify or recompute the FINGERPRINT and MESSAGE-INTEGRITY values, and transform the XOR-MAPPED-ADDRESS. Results must match the values shown in the RFC.

The vectors test the full message format including attribute ordering, message length calculations, and transaction IDs. Padding bytes within attributes must be handled correctly; the RFC notes that padding bytes may take any value (spaces in some vectors, null bytes in others), so implementations must skip them.

Message order matters: MESSAGE-INTEGRITY and FINGERPRINT must be computed and verified in the correct sequence relative to other attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: Write down what your code produces for each message. If your answer matches the answer in the document, congratulations! Your code is correct.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Test vectors themselves pose no security risk. However, implementers must ensure their STUN implementations correctly compute FINGERPRINT (CRC32), MESSAGE-INTEGRITY (HMAC-SHA1), and XOR-MAPPED-ADDRESS transformations. Any errors in these cryptographic operations would allow an attacker to forge STUN messages or intercept address translations.

The sample messages in this RFC include credentials and authentication codes. These are fictional test values generated specifically for the RFC and should never be used in production systems.
sections.plainLanguage: These are fake passwords just for testing. Real systems must keep their actual secrets safe from attackers.
